repos.title: LlamaFactory: Unified Efficient Fine-Tuning of 100+ Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
LlamaFactory is a unified framework integrating efficient fine-tuning methods to adapt over 100 large language models without custom code. It comprises three modules: a Model Loader attaching adapters like LoRA, QLoRA, and GaLore; a Data Worker standardizing dataset formats; and a Trainer supporting pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, and DPO. A key feature is model-sharing RLHF, which uses dynamic adapter switching to run the full pipeline on a single pre-trained model. The web interface LlamaBoard allows users to configure experiments and monitor training in real time.

The authors validate the framework on an NVIDIA A100 GPU using Gemma-2B, Llama2-7B, and Llama2-13B. On a corpus of roughly 400K tokens from PubMed abstracts, 4-bit QLoRA reduces peak memory to 5.21 GB for Gemma-2B compared to 17.06 GB for full tuning, while LoRA achieves a throughput of 3521 tokens/s. In downstream text generation tasks with 2,000 training examples, LoRA and QLoRA generally match or exceed full-tuning ROUGE scores across eight instruction-tuned models. Limitations include the requirement for adapter-based methods when using quantized weights and the fact that full-tuning Llama2-13B exceeds the 40GB memory limit of the test hardware.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning large language models is costly, so LlamaFactory unifies efficient fine-tuning methods in one framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing fine-tuning frameworks support fewer efficient methods than LlamaFactory, as its feature comparison shows.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques
digest_headlines.headline: The paper groups efficient fine-tuning into optimization methods, such as LoRA, and computation methods, such as flash attention.

digest_headlines.heading: LlamaFactory Framework
digest_headlines.headline: LlamaFactory has three modules, Model Loader, Data Worker and Trainer, with a web interface called LlamaBoard.

digest_headlines.heading: Empirical Study
digest_headlines.headline: Across tested models, quantized low-rank adaptation used the least memory and low-rank adaptation scored best on most generation tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Future work targets more modalities, parallel training strategies and stronger methods for conversational models.

digest_headlines.heading: Broader Impact and Responsible Use
digest_headlines.headline: The authors expect the framework to benefit open-source communities, and require users to follow model licenses.

repos.title: OpenVoice: Versatile Instant Voice Cloning
repos.paper_summary: OpenVoice is an instant voice cloning system that copies a speaker's tone color from a short reference clip while separately controlling emotion, accent, rhythm, pauses, intonation, and language. It splits the task into a base speaker TTS model (a modified VITS that takes style and language embeddings) and a feed-forward tone color converter. The converter uses an encoder, an invertible normalizing flow conditioned on a tone color vector, and HiFi-GAN decoding. The flow is trained with a KL loss against IPA phoneme features, which removes tone color from the content representation; the reference tone color is then inserted by running the flow in reverse. The base model was trained on about 30K sentences from four speakers, and the converter on 300K samples from 20K speakers. The paper reports no quantitative comparison against baselines; evaluation is qualitative, with audio on a demo site. Speed is 12× real-time on one A10G GPU (85 ms per second of speech). Cross-lingual cloning to unseen languages works when a base speaker exists for the target language. Limitations: emotion can be slightly neutralized in some cases, and the estimated 40× real-time upper bound is not yet reached.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Instant voice cloning needs a short reference clip, but existing methods lack style control and multi-language cloning without large multi-speaker data.

digest_headlines.heading: Approach
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVoice decouples a base speaker text-to-speech model for style and language from a tone color converter that adds the reference voice.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiment
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVoice is evaluated qualitatively rather than against baselines, reaching 12 times real-time speed on one graphics processing unit.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Decoupling tone color from style and language is presented as the core principle, with code and weights released.

repos.title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction
repos.paper_summary: Edge0 is a streaming inference engine for 35B-class mixture-of-experts models on a 24 GB consumer machine. Expert weights stay on SSD and are memory-mapped on demand, so peak memory tracks the active experts, not all parameters. A per-layer prerouter head predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead, so expert reads overlap the current forward pass. The prediction is used as the routing itself, so the staged experts match the routed experts and none are dropped. An unmerged int4 recovery LoRA, distilled from the fp16 teacher on the student routing path, recovers quality lost to quantization and routing replacement. On a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB, the 35B tier decodes at 20.4 tok/s with 2.9 GiB peak active memory, and the 8B tier at 28.0 tok/s with 1.5 GiB. On OpenCompass, the 35B tier averages 79.2 against 83.2 for its fp16 base, and the 8B tier 69.9 against 72.7. Limitations: AIME loses 6.1 points (35B) and 10.0 points (8B), requests are served one at a time, and CPU graph building sets a 44 ms per-step floor.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Storing 35B-class MoE weights on a 24 GB machine is the bottleneck, so Edge0 keeps experts on SSD and streams them.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior offloading moves the weight footprint rather than shrinking it, and pre-gating schedules next-block experts too late for a streaming engine.

digest_headlines.heading: System Design
digest_headlines.headline: A 40-layer MoE needs 16.9 GiB of routed experts, so Edge0 mmaps them from SSD across four executor paths.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Three training phases make the model work under replaced routing: head distillation, fine-tuning on the student path, and on-policy distillation.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Both tiers average within a few points of fp16 bases, and the prerouter adds +80 to +84% decode where weights do not fit.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Decode has a 44 ms per-step floor from graph building, quality loss concentrates in long-chain reasoning, and one backend exists.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A 35B MoE runs at 20 tok/s in 3 GiB on a 24 GB desktop, with framework, checkpoints, and adapters open source.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the softmax-top-k and sigmoid-group routing formulas and the incremental-stack assembly A/B results.

repos.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
repos.paper_summary:
DSPy is a programming model that compiles declarative language model pipelines into self-improving systems by automatically optimizing prompts and demonstrations. It replaces hard-coded prompt strings with parameterized modules, such as `ChainOfThought` or `ReAct`, which are optimized by "teleprompters." These optimizers bootstrap few-shot examples or finetune smaller models to maximize a user-defined metric.

On the GSM8K math word problem dataset, compiled DSPy programs using GPT-3.5 achieved 81.6% test accuracy, outperforming standard few-shot prompting (72.4%) and expert-created demonstrations (72.4%). For llama2-13b-chat, the best configuration reached 46.9% test accuracy, surpassing the zero-shot baseline of 9.4%. On HotPotQA multi-hop question answering, a compiled multi-hop program with GPT-3.5 achieved 45.6% answer exact match, while a finetuned T5-Large model reached 39.3% on the development set. The paper notes that compiling typically takes minutes to tens of minutes. Limitations include reliance on specific metrics for optimization and the fact that results are reported on only two case studies.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hand-written prompt templates for LM pipelines are brittle, and the paper proposes DSPy to replace them with optimizable modules.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing toolkits rely on hand-written prompt templates, while DSPy aims to optimize arbitrary multi-stage LM pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: The DSPy Programming Model
digest_headlines.headline: DSPy programs combine typed signatures, parameterized modules, and teleprompters that optimize all modules against a metric.

digest_headlines.heading: The DSPy Compiler
digest_headlines.headline: The compiler runs three stages: bootstrapping candidate demonstrations, selecting among them, and optimizing control flow.

digest_headlines.heading: Goals of Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: The evaluation hypothesizes that DSPy can replace hand-written prompts without losing quality, adapt across LMs, and enable richer pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: Case Study: Math Word Problems
digest_headlines.headline: Compiled DSPy programs improve GPT-3.5 and llama2-13b-chat on math word problems from 4–20% accuracy to 49–88%.

digest_headlines.heading: Case Study: Complex Question Answering
digest_headlines.headline: On HotPotQA, a multihop program compiled with ensembling reaches 54.7 dev answer exact match with GPT-3.5.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: DSPy supports rapid development of effective systems with small LMs, and wider task reporting is deferred to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers advanced signatures, a comparison with LangChain and LlamaIndex, and long prompts from existing libraries and DSPy.

repos.title: HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image
repos.paper_summary: HairDeck generates the stylized hair cards of a character and the spring-bone chains that animate them, from a point cloud or a single image. Each card is one continuous token from a card VAE, and a set diffusion transformer without positional embedding denoises all card tokens of a hairstyle together with flow matching; an existence flag on each token sets the card count. A second set DiT generates the spring-bone chains from the card tokens. Training uses 36,440 CHARM hairstyles from VRoid characters, plus synthetic style augmentation and renders restyled by an image-editing model. On CHARM's 100-hairstyle test set, Chamfer distance drops from 0.0117 (CHARM) to 0.0066 and orientation error from 40.0° to 16.8°, at 1.01 s per hairstyle against 33.7 s for CHARM. On 76 rendered single-image test characters, CD is 0.0089 against 0.0139 to 0.0186 for baselines, with a 3.5% failure rate against 13.2% to 34.2%. The paper states that very short hair and alpha-textured realistic cards are outside the training data, and that no textures are generated.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing generators do not output the artist-placed hair cards of stylized characters, so HairDeck generates each card as one token.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers strand hair, realistic cards, stylized characters and set generation, but CHARM is the only prior stylized card generator.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Each card is encoded as one continuous token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all tokens together without positional embedding.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On CHARM's test set HairDeck lowers Chamfer distance from 0.0117 to 0.0066 and orientation error from 40.0° to 16.8°, taking 1.01 s.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: HairDeck outputs card geometry without textures and learns only from stylized VRoid hairstyles, so short hair and realistic cards fall outside it.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists implementation settings, appearance augmentation, chain metrics, export, baseline details, and additional comparisons and results.

repos.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
repos.paper_summary:
AutoGen is an open-source framework for building LLM applications via multi-agent conversations. The system defines two core concepts: conversable agents, which are customizable entities backed by LLMs, tools, or human inputs, and conversation programming, a method that structures application logic around inter-agent message passing and control flow. Agents use unified interfaces to send messages and generate replies, with an auto-reply mechanism driving the workflow without a central controller. Developers can program interaction patterns using Python code or natural language instructions embedded in agent prompts.

The paper evaluates AutoGen across six domains. On the MATH dataset (5000 problems), the default two-agent configuration achieved 69.48% accuracy, outperforming vanilla GPT-4 at 55.18%. In ALFWorld decision-making tasks, adding a "grounding" agent improved performance by 15% over a ReAct baseline. For coding tasks on OptiGuide, a multi-agent design increased the F-1 score for identifying unsafe code by 8% with GPT-4 and 35% with GPT-3.5-turbo compared to a single-agent setup. The framework reduced the core workflow code for one application from 430 lines to 100 lines. Limitations include the reliance on proprietary models like GPT-4 for peak performance and the lack of formal safety guarantees for fully autonomous agent interactions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-agent conversation is proposed as the basis for building LLM applications, implemented in the AutoGen framework.

digest_headlines.heading: The AutoGen Framework
digest_headlines.headline: AutoGen rests on conversable agents and conversation programming, where agents exchange messages and control flow emerges from those conversations.

digest_headlines.heading: Applications of AutoGen
digest_headlines.headline: Six example applications test AutoGen across math, retrieval, decision making, coding, group chat and chess.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The discussion frames AutoGen as a general framework and states that its experiments are early, with safety questions left open.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics statement
digest_headlines.headline: The ethics statement names privacy, bias, accountability, trust and unintended consequences as risks to address.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work with a comparison table, expanded discussion, usage guidelines, future work, and supporting figures.

repos.title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models
repos.paper_summary: Plan-and-Solve (PS) Prompting is a zero-shot prompting strategy for large language models that instructs the model to devise a plan dividing a task into subtasks before executing them. The extended variant, PS+, adds instructions to extract relevant variables and calculate intermediate results. On ten datasets covering arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning using GPT-3 (text-davinci-003), PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT by an average of 6.3% on arithmetic tasks, reaching 76.7% accuracy compared to 70.4%. It also exceeds Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought on five of six arithmetic benchmarks. Error analysis on GSM8K shows PS+ reduces calculation errors from 7% to 5% and missing-step errors from 12% to 7%, though semantic misunderstanding errors remain at 27%. The paper notes two limitations: prompt sensitivity requires careful manual design, and the method does not address semantic understanding errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Zero-shot chain-of-thought errors are split into calculation, missing-step, and semantic errors, and a plan-based prompt targets two of them.

digest_headlines.heading: Plan-and-Solve Prompting
digest_headlines.headline: Plan-and-Solve prompting uses a zero-shot trigger that asks the model to devise and carry out a plan, followed by an answer-extraction prompt.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use ten benchmarks with text-davinci-003 and compare against zero-shot and few-shot baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Results
digest_headlines.headline: PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT on all arithmetic datasets and averages 76.7 against 77.6 for Manual-CoT.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work places Plan-and-Solve among chain-of-thought methods that use zero-shot prompting and planning.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that plan-based zero-shot prompting outperforms Zero-shot-CoT and matches few-shot CoT on some arithmetic datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Prompt design is labour-intensive and the method does not address semantic misunderstanding errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics
digest_headlines.headline: The paper lists the datasets and their licences and states that the prompts contain no personal information or discriminatory wording.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists trigger-sentence ablations for every dataset and example outputs from Zero-shot-PS+.

repos.title: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness
repos.paper_summary:
Prime Agent is an open-source harness for long-horizon evaluation and coding-agent workflows. It provides a persistent IPython REPL, recursive subagents with direct agent-to-agent communication, and Continual Harness for storing versioned prompts, memories, skills, and subagent specifications across trajectories. The model controls strategy construction while the runtime standardizes execution, recovery, and resource accounting.

The paper evaluates Prime Agent against native and alternative harnesses (Pi, Claude Code, Codex) on interactive reasoning, long-context tasks, and autonomous systems construction. On ARC-AGI-3, Prime Agent raises RHAE Best@1 from 30% to 95.5%. In long-context benchmarks, it matches or exceeds baselines; for example, on OOLONG (Yahoo, 128k), GPT-5.6 Sol scores .940 with Prime Agent versus .900 with Codex. For GPU kernel generation on PMPP-Hard, Prime Agent achieves comparable solve rates at substantially reduced token cost. A seven-day Factorio run completed 24 of 196 technologies using 23.4 million output tokens. Limitations include models' poor handling of irreversible actions and online refinement potentially preserving specification exploits as reusable skills.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent argues the harness should expose expressive primitives, so evaluation measures model capability rather than harness failures.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Prime Agent Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent splits information management from computation management across persistent sessions, a daemon and Continual Harness state.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent is generally competitive on long-context tasks and close to native harnesses on GPU-kernel generation.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work spans programmatic inference, coding-agent runtimes, ARC-AGI-3 systems and multi-agent communication, which Prime Agent combines.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Many harness capabilities remain underused because current models were not trained to operate them.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists three out-of-loop nanoGPT experiments, from Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Pro and a third model, plus an orchestration example.

repos.title: Deep Photo Style Transfer
repos.paper_summary: The paper introduces a deep-learning method for photographic style transfer that preserves the photorealism of the input image while accurately matching the color and texture of a reference style image. The approach extends the Neural Style algorithm by adding two constraints to the optimization objective. First, a photorealism regularization term ensures the transformation from input to output is locally affine in color space, preventing spatial distortions like wiggly edges. This term uses the Matting Laplacian matrix derived from the input image. Second, an augmented style loss incorporates semantic segmentation masks for both images, restricting style transfer between semantically equivalent regions (e.g., sky to sky) to prevent "spillover" artifacts. The method uses a pre-trained VGG-19 network, with content features from `conv4_2` and style features from layers `conv1_1` through `conv5_1`. Optimization runs in 3–5 minutes on an NVIDIA Titan X GPU. In user studies, the method produced photorealistic results comparable to global histogram transfer methods, but achieved higher style faithfulness than Reinhard et al., Pitié et al., and Photoshop Match Color in over 80% of comparisons. Limitations include failure cases under extreme semantic mismatch between input and reference, which require manual segmentation masks to resolve.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Photographic style transfer must avoid painting-like distortion while keeping the reference style faithful.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method adds a locally affine color regularizer and semantic segmentation masks to Neural Style optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation Details
digest_headlines.headline: The implementation uses a pretrained convolutional network, two-stage optimization and merged segmentation classes.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Comparison
digest_headlines.headline: Compared with Neural Style, patch-based and global transfer methods, the approach avoids distortion and was judged most faithful more than 80% of the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: The approach transfers reference style faithfully across time of day, weather, season and artistic edits while keeping outputs photorealistic.

repos.title: Watch Your Step: Anticipated Perception for Humanoid Locomotion
repos.paper_summary: Watch Your Step introduces a perceptive locomotion framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid in which a lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts the next two footholds from proprioception and the velocity command, and the policy observes only small 7×7 elevation-map patches around those predicted footholds. The FPM is an MLP with two 128-unit hidden layers, trained by Huber regression on labeled footholds from recent policy rollouts and refit every 500 PPO iterations, jointly with a PPO locomotion policy. On the training terrain curriculum, the FPM policy reaches level 5 after 7.5k iterations, against 26.1k for the complete-map baseline (HM) and 20.0k for an attention-based encoder (AME2). AME2 ends slightly higher at 40k iterations but needs four GPUs and 6.3 s per policy update versus 0.55 s. In simulation, the FPM policy achieves 74.2% success on sparse corridor terrain versus 71.7% for AME2 and at most 42.7% for the other baselines, and 77.7% on out-of-distribution gaps. The policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 on stairs, a 0.55 m gap, and a 0.6 m drop. Limitations include reliance on an elevation map and that the policy's cautious behavior near unseen gaps is a hypothesis rather than a measured result.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Predicting footholds from proprioception and filtering the elevation map around them should cut redundant input for perceptive humanoid locomotion.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: The locomotion task is set as a reinforcement learning problem for a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid trained with PPO in 8192 parallel environments.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A blind foothold predictor is retrained periodically, and the policy sees only small height patches around its two predicted footholds.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments and Results
digest_headlines.headline: The gated policy reaches curriculum level 5 in 7.5k iterations, 3.4 to 3.5 times faster than full-map methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The approach trails full-map methods on stepped corridor terrain and cannot see obstacles approaching from the side.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Sampling the elevation map around predicted footholds learns faster than full-map policies and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1.
